title: The Udasis
hook: an ascetic order tracing itself to Sri Chand, which cared for many gurdwaras in hard times

segments.voice: Yesterday, sampardaa: a tradition handed on, one of many streams in the panth. Your line was many streams, one guru. Whose way of doing a shared thing did you ask about? Day one thousand three hundred three.

A family leaves home in a hurry, and a neighbor promises to look after the house. Months go by. Then years. The neighbor waters the plants, sweeps the step, opens the windows on hot days so the place can breathe. When the family finally comes back, the lamp in the front room is still lit. Nobody stood guard with a weapon. Somebody just kept showing up. The Sikh panth tells a story with that shape, about its own shrines. And the neighbors in it belong to an order you met in year three, through the Guru's son.
screen: `A FAMILY LEAVES IN A HURRY.` → `A NEIGHBOR KEEPS THE HOUSE.` → `THE LAMP STILL LIT.`

segments.voice: Start with who they are. The Udasis are an order of renunciants. They trace themselves to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, who chose a celibate life of meditation, as year three told. Udasi teachers kept Guru Nanak's hymns at the center of their devotion, and tradition remembers the later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect. Now the hard times. Year three walked through the years when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted, when riders lived in forests and on horseback, and could not safely stay near their own shrines. Tradition says that in those years Udasi caretakers looked after many gurdwaras. They didn't wear the Khalsa's outward form, so they could stay where Khalsa Sikhs could not. They kept the doors open, the lamps lit, and the Guru's word read. That is the heart of today's line: keepers in hard times. There's a second chapter, and it belongs here too. Tradition also remembers that, much later, at some shrines the hereditary caretakers grew wealthy and careless, and a reform movement brought those shrines back under the panth's own care. That story comes on another day. Hold both chapters together; one doesn't erase the other. Last, a line from Guru Nanak that sits close to the word udasi, which carries the sense of being detached. In the conversation with the Siddhas, the yogis of the mountains, he gives a picture of detachment, here in paraphrase: like a lotus that floats untouched by the water, like a duck that swims the stream and stays dry. The Udasis chose a renunciant's road to seek that freedom. In the hard years, their freedom from house and household left them free to keep the Guru's house.
screen: `AN ORDER TRACED TO BABA SRI CHAND.` · `THE HARD YEARS: KHALSA SIKHS HUNTED.` · `UDASIS KEPT THE LAMPS LIT.` · `THE LOTUS UNTOUCHED BY THE WATER.` · then, large: `KEEPERS IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: respect a quiet order. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who kept something going without being noticed: a grandparent who held the family's prayers, a caretaker at a place of worship, a neighbor who watched the house. You don't have to agree with every choice they made. Just see what they kept, and what might have been lost without them. Breathe in their name. Breathe out a little thanks. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Udasi. A renunciant order tracing itself to Baba Sri Chand. Tradition says Udasi caretakers kept many gurdwaras open when Khalsa Sikhs could not. Today's word.

Your line: keepers in hard times. Today, thank one person who quietly keeps something going, a place, a ritual, a group chat, a garden, and tell them what it would be like without them. Day one thousand three hundred three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Udasis as caretakers of many gurdwaras in the years when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted, and hold a range of views about the order's place in the panth today.

original.note: Punjabi: one who is detached, a renunciant. Guru Nanak's great journeys are also called his udasis.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Udasis are a footnote, the order of the son who wasn't chosen.

notes: Udasi custodianship of gurdwaras in the eighteenth century is given as 'tradition says'; the reason ('they didn't wear the Khalsa's outward form, so they could stay') is the usual explanation. Please confirm.

The later chapter (hereditary mahants and the gurdwara reform movement of the early twentieth century) is mentioned without names or dates and deferred to another day; please confirm the framing is fair to the Udasis and to the reformers.
Sidh Gosht, Ang 938: 'jaise jal meh kamal niraalam, murgaaee nai saane' paraphrased as a lotus untouched by the water and a duck that swims and stays dry. Please confirm Ang and paraphrase.
'udasi carries the sense of being detached' is given as the word's sense, not an etymology; please confirm.
Year three (day 729) introduced Sri Chand and the word Udasi; today avoids repeating that angle and focuses on custodianship. Day 1198 already used Sri Chand's meeting with Guru Ram Das.

Editor (y4 pass): claims rule; 'the century when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted' became 'the years', and 'Tradition and history both remember' became 'Tradition also remembers' (no unsourced historical claim).
